# Picsart's Reshoot: AI Video Editing That Swaps the Subject, Keeps the Take

> **In short:** Picsart says its new Reshoot node inside Flow uses AI to swap the people, products, or places in a video while preserving the original take. You give it a clip, reference images, and a short note about what should change.

You've got a great 15-second product clip filmed at your desk — the framing is perfect, your hands move at exactly the right moment, but the background looks messy. Re-shooting means setting everything up again and hoping you nail it twice. Picsart's new Reshoot tool, announced as a node inside its Flow editor, is built for exactly this kind of problem.

## What Reshoot actually does

Reshoot is **AI video-to-video editing** — a phrase worth slowing down on. In regular video editing, you cut and arrange clips; the footage stays the same. In video-to-video editing, an AI model re-generates the video so the contents look different, even though the underlying timing and camera movement stay the same.

According to Picsart's announcement, Reshoot re-shoots a video with new people, products, or places. You keep the **take** (in video language, a single continuous recording — the camera motion, the length, the framing) while changing what appears in the frame. Think of it like asking an AI to re-paint the scene while following the exact same choreography.

## How the workflow works

Picsart describes the process in three moves:

1. **Connect a clip** — the original video you want to re-render.
2. **Add a few reference images** — pictures of the person, product, or place you want to see instead.
3. **Write a short note** about what should change.

Flow then re-renders the clip with the new contents while holding onto the original take. That's the idea as Picsart presents it. The exact menus and button names inside Flow aren't something I can map out step by step — once you open the editor, you'll see the Reshoot option where new nodes appear.

## What it keeps vs. what it changes

| Keeps | Changes |
|---|---|
| Camera movement | People in the scene |
| Clip length and pacing | Products on the table |
| Framing and angles | Background and location |

This is the practical promise: you don't have to re-record to try a different version.

## What this means for you

- **If you create content for fun or social media**: Reshoot is a fast way to test a few different versions of the same clip — different outfits, different rooms, different props — without setting up multiple shoots.
- **If you run a small business or work in marketing**: think product demos, store tours, or staff introductions filmed once and then re-themed for different campaigns, seasons, or audiences.
- **If you're new to AI video tools**: this is a good first experiment because the inputs (a clip plus reference images) are simple. Expect imperfect results on the first try — generative video still gets hands, reflections, and small text wrong sometimes.
- **If you already use Picsart Flow**: drop Reshoot into the same canvas you use for other nodes and pair it with strong, well-lit reference shots — vague change notes produce vague results.

## Wrap-up

Reshoot turns a single filmed clip into the starting point for many versions, which is exactly the part of video production that usually eats the most time. Open Picsart Flow, find the Reshoot node, and try a 10-second test clip first — something simple, like swapping the mug on your desk for a different one. That's the cheapest way to see what the tool does well and where it stumbles.
